general-terms-content.description: Commonly used Japanese terms in a martial arts context.

dojo.name: Dojo
dojo.english: Training hall, place of the way

sensei.name: Sensei
sensei.english: Teacher, instructor (one who has gone before)

karate.name: Karate
karate.details: Martial art, fighting art, the art in which both body and mind are trained for (daily) health; in emergencies it is a self-defense art that does not use weapons. Literally: 'empty hand'. This martial art was previously referred to as 'Tode'.

karate-do.name: Karatedo
karate-do.english: The way of the empty hand
karate-do.details: Like 'Karate'. Literally: 'the way of the empty hand'. The addition 'do' is commonly used to emphasize the mental and spiritual development of the practitioner.

okinawa.name: Okinawa
okinawa.english: Largest island of the Ryukyu islands
okinawa.details: Largest island of the Ryukyu islands south of Japan off the coast of China, which politically belongs to Japan. Okinawa is more than 100 km long and between 5 and 20 km wide. This is where karate was originally developed, with Chinese Kempo as an important source, such as crane boxing.

nahate.name: Nahate
nahate.english: Old name for the martial art in Naha
nahate.details: Old name for the martial art practiced in the town of Naha in Okinawa. Besides Goyu-ryu, this is also the basis for karate styles such as Uechi-ryu and Pangai-noon-ryu.

shurite-tomarite.name: Shurite and Tomarite
shurite-tomarite.english: Old names for martial arts from Shuri and Tomari
shurite-tomarite.details: Old names for martial arts from the Okinawan towns of Shuri and Tomari (these are now districts of the metropolis Naha); the basis of several other karate styles. In Japan, Shotokan and Wado ryu originated from a combination of Shuri-te and Tomari-te. Kyokushin Kai-karate emerged from Shotokan and Goju Kai.

kobudo.name: Kobudo
kobudo.details: Okinawan martial art that uses 'weapons' (most commonly used: 183 cm staff (Bo), (small) trident (Sai), two sticks connected by a chain (Nunchaku, flail), sickle-shaped wooden weapon (Kama) and sword (Katana)).

kempo-hakku.name: Kempo Hakku
kempo-hakku.english: The eight laws of the fist
kempo-hakku.details: Poem 'The eight laws of the fist'.

budo.name: Budo
budo.details: The 'way of the warrior' as a lifestyle/philosophy/(life's)way.

kenkon.name: Kenkon
kenkon.details: Literally: 'heaven and earth'; symbol of the International Okinawan Goju-ryu Karate-do Federation (IOGKF). It was conceived by Chojun Miyagi, founder of Goju-Ryu karate. In the Netherlands, Goju-Ryu was introduced by Harry de Spa.

tanden.name: Tanden
tanden.details: Energetic and psycho-physical center of the body. In a natural stance, the tanden is located at the midpoint of the body.

hara.name: Hara
hara.details: Literally: 'lower abdomen', in practice the same as tanden.

ki.name: Ki
ki.details: (The experience of) Vital energy or life force; often referred to with concepts such as breathing energy, breathing power, etc., also translated as 'spirit'. Manifestation of the unity of body, breath and spirit. In Chinese referred to as Qi.

chinkuchi-kakin.name: Chinkuchi Kakin (Kimae)
chinkuchi-kakin.details: Directing force; short and focused tension of the muscles at the moment of impact.

muchimi.name: Muchimi
muchimi.details: Slow, flowing, heavy, sticky, controlled and concentrated movement.

chiru-no-chan-chan.name: Chiru No Chan Chan
chiru-no-chan-chan.details: Explosive force, spring force, starting force, initial force, push-off force or initial impulse. It relates to the force exerted at the beginning of the movement, which (also) comes from a reaction to an opponent's movement.

chikara.name: Chikara
chikara.details: Power, lively and powerful movement; movement that is charged by 'ki'.

chikara-no-nujisashi.name: Chikara No Nujisashi
chikara-no-nujisashi.details: Alternation between tension and relaxation. More extensively: the entering and exiting of force, in conjunction with the alternation of tension and relaxation. The term 'nujisashi' separately is used for the calmer, more controlled parts of the kata.

shimejurasan.name: Shimejurasan
shimejurasan.details: The perfect execution of the kata.

te-no-omoi.name: Te No Omoi (Te No Omomi)
te-no-omoi.details: Literally: 'heavy hands'. The impact of the technique in Te no omomi comes from the weight and acceleration given to a hand (arm) or foot (leg).

kiai.name: Kiai (or Yagui)
kiai.details: Shout, where the force is concentrated and directed (literally: 'coming together or harmonization of life force and spirit').

ma.name: Ma
ma.details: Internal timing; performing the technique in accordance with the rhythm of the synchronization of body, breath and spirit.

zanshin.name: Zanshin
zanshin.details: Lingering attention and alertness, fighting attention. Literally: 'lingering heart'.

haragei.name: Haragei
haragei.details: The confidence felt in the lower abdomen to handle (engage with) any situation. Literally: 'the approach from your hara'.

isshin.name: Isshin
isshin.details: Complete devotion, one point of attention. Literally: 'one heart'.

kokyu.name: Kokyu
kokyu.details: Breath, also breath, body and spirit.

seiza.name: Seiza

stances-content.description: Basic karate stances used in Goju Ryu. Each stance has a specific purpose and contributes to movement, defense, and offense.
stances-content.title: Stances

seiza.name: Seiza
seiza.details: Seiza is the traditional, formal and polite Japanese way of sitting on the floor, kneeling. It's a fundamental posture both in Karate and in Japanese culture. This stance is used to perform the formal 'floor bow' called zarei.
seiza.instructions: Instructions: Place your knees on the floor with your feet underneath you. Sit down on your feet with your back straight. Place your hands on your thighs with your thumbs close together.

musubi-dachi.name: Musubi Dachi
musubi-dachi.details: Musubi Dachi is the formal way of standing in Japanese martial arts and in Japan. This stance is very important and is used to perform the formal respectful bow called rei. Musubi Dachi and rei should be performed before and after warmups, kihon, kata, kumite or any interaction between people.
musubi-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet together and toes pointing forward. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands at your sides with fingers pointing down.

heisoku-dachi.name: Heisoku Dachi
heisoku-dachi.details: Heisoku Dachi is the ready stance used in some kata. It is similar to musubi-dachi, but the feet are kept together.
heisoku-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet together and toes pointing forward. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands at your sides with fingers pointing down.

heiko-dachi.name: Heiko Dachi
heiko-dachi.details: Heiko Dachi is an attention stance or 'get ready' stance used in some styles. It is generally performed after bowing (musubi-dachi), right before kihon practice or kata. Heiko Dachi is also the stance performed when listening to instructions.
heiko-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes pointing forward. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands at your sides with fingers pointing down.

hachiji-dachi.name: Hachiji Dachi
hachiji-dachi.details: Hachiji Dachi, also known as yoi-dachi is a formal waiting posture used in some styles of Karate. Hachiji Dachi can also be used after standing bowing of while performing tsuki. 'Yoi' posture is not common in Okinawan Karate.
hachiji-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes pointing outward at about 45 degrees. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands at your sides with fingers pointing down.

kiba-dachi.name: Kiba Dachi
kiba-dachi.details: Kiba Dachi is a fundamental position of Karate that not only used to practice basic strikes like the seiken tsuki, but that can be integrated into self-defense or kumite practice as well. This is a very strong stance for defending against side attacks. Kiba Dachi is a posture that strengthens the legs, the back and to some extent, the core.
kiba-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet wide apart, about twice shoulder-width. Bend your knees and lower your body down. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips with elbows close to your body.

shiko-dachi.name: Shiko Dachi
shiko-dachi.details: Shiko Dachi, also known as the 'square stance' is pretty much the same as Kiba dachi but the feet are open at about 45° angle.
shiko-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet wide apart, about twice shoulder-width, with toes pointing outward at about 45 degrees. Bend your knees and lower your body down. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips with elbows close to your body.

sanchin-dachi.name: Sanchin Dachi
sanchin-dachi.details: Sanchin Dachi is a fundamental Karate posture that offers great stability and rooting. The majority of Japanese styles like Shotokan use this stance only in kata, but Okinawan styles uses it for self-defense and kumite, particularly Naha-te styles like Goju-Ryu and Uechi-Ryu.
sanchin-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes pointing inward. Bend your knees and lower your body down. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips with elbows close to your body.

zenkutsu-dachi.name: Zenkutsu Dachi
zenkutsu-dachi.details: Zenkutsu Dachi, a.k.a. forward stance, is one of the most common stances in Karate. It's a stance that allows you to reach far and generate a great deal of power generation moving forward. Like with most stances, the Japanese version of Zenkutsu Dachi tends to be very long and wide compared to the shorter, more natural Okinawan version.
zenkutsu-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Take a step forward with your front foot. Bend your front knee so it's over your front foot. Keep your back leg straight and lower your body down. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips.

han-zenkutsu-dachi.name: Han Zenkutsu Dachi
han-zenkutsu-dachi.details: Han Zenkutsu Dachi is the shorter or half version of Zenkutsu Dachi. It's a stance suitable for self-defense and kumite or sparring as it offers greater mobility. Han Zenkutsu Dachi is a neutral stance that allows you to quickly move back into the defensive Neko-ashi-dachi or the thrust forward into a full Zenkutsu Dachi or Sanchin Dachi.
han-zenkutsu-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Take a shorter step forward with your front foot compared to full zenkutsu-dachi. Bend your front knee slightly so it's over your front foot. Keep your back leg bent and lower your body down. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips.

kokutsu-dachi.name: Kokutsu Dachi
kokutsu-dachi.details: Kokutsu Dachi is a defensive position that allows you to quickly retreat or move back and counterattack. It's great to evade attack from your opponent.
kokutsu-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Take a step back with your back foot. Bend your back knee and lower your body down. Keep your front leg straight. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips.

neko-ashi-dachi.name: Neko Ashi Dachi
neko-ashi-dachi.details: Neko Ashi Dachi is a great defensive stance as most of the weight is on the back leg, allowing counterattack with kicks and quick sideways evasions. Sadly unpopular with karateka this stance as perfectly suited for both self-defense and kumite.
neko-ashi-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Place most of your weight on your back leg. Bend your back knee and lower your body down. Keep your front leg straight with toes pointing forward. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips.

tsuru-ashi-dachi.name: Tsuru Ashi Dachi
tsuru-ashi-dachi.details: Tsuru Ashi Dachi is a stance used to avoid attacks and to transition into other techniques.
tsuru-ashi-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand on one leg with your other leg bent at the knee. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips with elbows close to your body.

kosa-dachi.name: Kosa Dachi
kosa-dachi.details: The cross stance is generally performed for turning, dodging to the side or when landing from a jump.
kosa-dachi.instructions: Instructions: Stand with your feet crossed, one foot in front of the other. Bend your knees slightly and lower your body down. Keep your back straight and head high. Place your hands in fists at your hips with elbows close to your body.

age-uke.name: Age Uke
age-uke.details: Age Uke (Rising Block) is a fundamental upward blocking technique used to defend against attacks to the face or upper body. The forearm moves upwards to deflect the attack, while the other hand is withdrawn to the hip in preparation for a counter-attack.

gedan-barai.name: Gedan Barai
gedan-barai.details: Gedan Barai (Downward Sweep Block) is a sweeping downward block that defends against low attacks. The arm moves in a downward arc to deflect strikes aimed at the lower body, with the other arm retracting to the hip position.

soto-uke.name: Soto Uke
soto-uke.details: Soto Uke (Outside Block) is an outside-to-inside block used to deflect attacks coming from the outside. The forearm moves from outside to inside in a horizontal path to redirect the opponent's strike.

uchi-uke.name: Uchi Uke
uchi-uke.details: Uchi Uke (Inside Block) is an inside-to-outside block used to deflect attacks coming from the inside. The forearm moves from inside to outside in a horizontal path.

shuto-uke.name: Shuto Uke
shuto-uke.details: Shuto Uke (Knife Hand Block) is performed using the edge of the hand (shuto). It can be used to block attacks to the midsection or head, often with a circular motion.

empi-uke.name: Empi Uke
empi-uke.details: Empi Uke (Elbow Block) uses the elbow to block an incoming attack, often effective at close range and against strikes to the body.

kosa-uke.name: Kosa Uke
kosa-uke.details: Kosa Uke (Cross Block) involves crossing the wrists or forearms to create a barrier against an attack. It can be performed at various heights (jodan, chudan, gedan).

juji-uke.name: Juji Uke
juji-uke.details: Juji Uke (X-Block) uses the arms crossed in an 'X' shape to block an attack, typically a downward strike or kick. The hands can be open or closed.

haiwan-uke.name: Haiwan Uke
haiwan-uke.details: Haiwan Uke (Back Arm Block) uses the back of the forearm to block an incoming technique. It is often used to deflect strikes coming towards the side of the body or head.

osae-uke.name: Osae Uke
osae-uke.details: Osae Uke (Pressing Block) is a technique that presses down or pins an opponent's attack, often used to control an opponent's limb or create an opening.
